facts.statement: Decisions usually cannot be based on the whole population because of its size, the time and the expense (for example one cannot open and test every packet of milk a plant produces), so a representative sample is taken, tested, and the result generalised to the whole. Complete enumeration, or census, is used only where practical, as in the population census held every ten years.

A population is all the items to be studied, and a sample is a part of it selected to represent the whole. Measures such as the mean and standard deviation are called statistics when they describe a sample and parameters when they describe a population. By convention, Roman letters denote sample statistics and Greek or capital letters denote population parameters: population size N, mean mu and standard deviation sigma; sample size n and mean x-bar.

The units under study are sampling units and the number of units in a sample is the sample size. Samples are chosen by non-random (judgement) or random (probability) methods. In probability sampling every item in the population has a chance of being chosen; in judgement sampling personal knowledge or opinion decides which items are included. Judgement samples are convenient and useful as pilot or trial samples, but the rigorous statistical analysis possible with random probability samples cannot be done with them, and a judgement sample that loses much representativeness has bought convenience at a high price.

A biased sample arises when respondents are chosen from people who hold strong feelings on the issue (for example interviewing only those most affected by a proposed law). A report from a biased sample does not reflect true opinion. With random sampling the reliability of the estimates can be determined statistically, which avoids such errors.

The four main types of random sampling are simple random, systematic, stratified and cluster. Simple random sampling gives each possible sample an equal probability of being picked and each item in the population an equal chance of inclusion. From a population of four (A, B, C, D) there are six possible samples of two, each with probability 1/6, and each member appears in three of the six samples, so each has probability 1/2 of being in the sample.
facts.locator: Printed p. 20, section 2.2 Random Sampling, Simple Random Sampling

facts.statement: Sampling without replacement means a sampled item is not returned to the population, so no item can appear twice in the sample; sampling with replacement returns the item after it is noted, so the same item may be drawn more than once. An infinite population, as used in practice, is one that cannot be enumerated in a reasonable period of time; the theoretical concept approximates a very large finite population.
facts.locator: Printed p. 21, Simple Random Sampling and glossary p. 39

facts.statement: Slips drawn from a box work for small groups but poorly for large populations. A random sample can instead be drawn with random numbers, generated by a computer programmed to scramble numbers or taken from a table of random digits in which every digit from 0 to 9 is equally likely and every sequence of a given length is equally likely. Each member is given a number (for example 00 to 99 for 100 employees) and the numbers read from the table choose the sample.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 21-22, How to do Random Sampling

facts.statement: In systematic sampling elements are selected from the population at a uniform interval measured in time, order or space: a random starting point is chosen in the first interval and every k-th element after it is taken (for example every twentieth name in a directory). Each element has an equal chance of selection but each possible sample does not (taking every tenth employee from a random start means employees numbered 2, 3, 4 and 5 can never be selected together). It carries a risk of error when the interval coincides with a pattern in the population (for example checking restaurant eating on Fridays only), but it can save time and cost compared with simple random sampling.

In stratified sampling the population is divided into relatively homogeneous groups called strata, and elements are chosen at random from each stratum either in numbers proportional to the stratum's share of the population or in equal numbers whose results are then weighted by that share. It suits a population already divided into groups of different sizes (social class, age group), and a properly designed stratified sample reflects the characteristics of the population more accurately than other kinds of samples.
facts.locator: Printed p. 23, Stratified Sampling, and glossary p. 38

facts.statement: In cluster sampling the population is divided into groups or clusters, assumed individually representative of the whole, a random sample of clusters is chosen and every unit in the chosen clusters is examined (for example dividing a city into blocks and interviewing every household in selected blocks). A well-designed cluster sample can be more precise than a simple random sample at considerably less cost. Stratified sampling is used when each group has small variation within itself but there is wide variation between groups; cluster sampling is used in the opposite case, when there is considerable variation within each group but the groups are essentially similar.
facts.locator: Printed p. 23, Cluster Sampling and Comparison of Stratified and Cluster Sampling

facts.statement: Each sample drawn from a population has its own mean, so the sample mean varies from sample to sample. A sampling distribution is the distribution of all possible values of a statistic from all possible samples of a given size drawn from the population; there is a sampling distribution of the mean, of the median and of a proportion. For a population of five heights (160, 162, 164, 170, 156 cm) the ten possible samples of three have means that range from 159.33 to 165.00, narrower than the population range 156 to 170, and whose average, 162.40, equals the population mean.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 24-25 and 28, section 2.3 and Table 2.3

facts.statement: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean is called the standard error of the mean, and in general the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic is its standard error. It measures how far sample means vary because of chance in the sampling process (sampling error), and so indicates the accuracy to expect when a sample statistic estimates a population value; a statistic with a smaller standard error is a better estimator.
facts.locator: Printed p. 25, Concept of Standard Error

facts.statement: If the population is normally distributed, the sampling distribution of the mean is also normal, with mean equal to the population mean (mu of x-bar = mu) and standard deviation equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size (sigma of x-bar = sigma / sqrt(n)). Enlarging the sample from 3 to 4 leaves the population standard deviation unchanged but reduces the standard deviation of the sampling distribution.
facts.locator: Printed p. 28, section 2.4 Sampling from Normal Populations

facts.statement: To find a probability for a sample mean, convert it to a standard normal value z = (x-bar - mu) / (standard error) and read the standard normal table of areas between 0 and z. Areas for values on the same side of zero are subtracted (larger minus smaller); for values on opposite sides they are added. In the courseware's illustration, savings balances with mean Rs 2,000 and standard deviation Rs 600 sampled with n = 100 give a standard error of Rs 60, and the probability that the mean lies between Rs 1,900 and Rs 2,050 is 0.4525 + 0.2967 = 0.7492 (z of -1.67 and 0.83).

When the population is not normal the mean of the sampling distribution of the mean still equals the population mean. The central limit theorem says that the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as the sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution. A very large sample is not needed: the normal distribution is used as an approximation whenever the sample size is at least 30, and the distribution can be nearly normal with samples of even half that size. The theorem lets sample statistics be used for inference about population parameters without knowing the shape of the population distribution.

As the standard error falls, any sample mean is likely to be closer to the population mean and the precision of the sample mean as an estimator rises. Because the standard error varies inversely with the square root of n, there is a diminishing return in sampling: with sigma = 100, n = 10 gives a standard error of 31.63 and n = 100 gives 10, so a tenfold larger sample reduces the standard error to about one-third. Larger samples cost more, so managers should weigh the extra precision against the extra cost.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 35-36 and 37-38, Relationship between Sample Size and Standard Error

facts.statement: The formula sigma / sqrt(n) applies when the population is infinite or when sampling is with replacement. For a finite population sampled without replacement the standard error of the mean is (sigma / sqrt(n)) x sqrt((N - n) / (N - 1)), where N is the population size and n the sample size; the square-root term is the finite population multiplier. In the courseware illustration, 20 firms, sigma 75 and n = 5 give a multiplier of 0.888 and reduce the standard error from 33.54 to 29.8.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 36-37, section 2.7, and equations 3 and 4 on pp. 39-40

facts.statement: The sampling fraction is n/N, the share of the population contained in the sample. When the sampling fraction is small the multiplier is close to 1 (1,000 items with a sample of 20 give 0.99), and the generally accepted rule is that when the sampling fraction is less than 0.05 the finite population multiplier need not be used. Precision depends on the absolute size of the sample, not on the fraction of the population sampled.

payload.title: Why banks sample, and the symbols that go with it
payload.core_explanation_md:
Studying every item is rarely possible: the population may be huge, testing may destroy the item, and time and money are limited. So you take a **sample**, measure it, and generalise to the **population**. A full count (a **census**) is the exception.

Keep the notation straight; the letter tells you which world a number belongs to:

| | Population | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Size | N | n |
| Mean | mu | x-bar |
| Standard deviation | sigma | s |
| Name of such a number | parameter | statistic |

Sampling is only as good as the sample: if it is not representative, every conclusion drawn from it is shaky.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Why this matters in a bank: a credit-quality review of 20 lakh loan accounts cannot read every file. A sample read carefully tells more than a census read carelessly, provided the sample is well chosen.

self_check.prompt_text: From memory: which letters stand for population size, sample size, population mean and sample mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: N, n, mu and x-bar respectively.

payload.title: Judgement samples, random samples and bias
payload.core_explanation_md:
There are two ways to choose a sample.

| | Judgement (non-random) | Random (probability) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who picks | Someone's knowledge or opinion | Chance, with known probabilities |
| Strength | Quick, convenient, good for a pilot | Every item has a chance of selection |
| Weakness | Its validity cannot be tested; rigorous statistical analysis is not possible | Needs a list of the population and more effort |

**Bias** creeps in when you pick the people most likely to have strong views, for example surveying only those directly affected by a policy. The report then describes that group, not the public. Random selection avoids this, and it allows the reliability of the estimate to be worked out.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A judgement sample is not worthless: a branch manager choosing three typical branches to pilot a new form is sensible. The mistake is treating the pilot result as if it were a scientifically drawn sample.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can the reliability of an estimate be worked out for a random sample but not for a judgement sample?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Random selection gives known chances of inclusion, so statistical theory applies; a judgement sample depends on the chooser's opinion, so its representativeness cannot be tested.

payload.title: Simple random sampling: equal chances, with or without replacement
payload.core_explanation_md:
In **simple random sampling** every possible sample has the same chance of being picked, and so does every member of the population.

Small example: from four officers A, B, C, D choose two. There are six possible pairs (AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD), each with probability 1/6, and each officer is in three of the six, so each has a 1/2 chance of being chosen.

Two ways to draw:

- **Without replacement**: a chosen item is set aside, so it cannot appear twice.
- **With replacement**: the item is put back before the next draw, so it can be chosen again.

For big populations, slips in a box do not work. Give each member a number and read numbers from a computer or a table of random digits, where every digit from 0 to 9 is equally likely.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: An "infinite" population in statistics does not mean literally infinite. It means one too large to list in reasonable time, treated as if it never runs out.

self_check.prompt_text: Five officers, sample of two without replacement. How many possible samples are there, and what is the chance that a particular officer is in the sample?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ten possible samples; each officer is in four of them, so the chance is 4/10 = 2/5.

payload.title: Systematic sampling: every k-th item from a random start
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Before using it, scan the list for any cycle (weekly, monthly, alphabetical clusters). If one matches your interval, change the interval or switch methods.

self_check.prompt_text: Name one advantage and one risk of systematic sampling.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Advantage: it can save time and cost. Risk: an interval matching a pattern in the population biases the sample.

payload.title: Stratified or cluster sampling: which one, and why
payload.core_explanation_md:
Both start by dividing the population into groups. They differ in what the groups look like, and so in what you do next.

| | Stratified | Cluster |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Groups | **Strata**: similar inside, different from each other | **Clusters**: much alike each other, varied inside |
| What you sample | Items at random from **every** stratum | A random few clusters, then **every** item in them |
| How many from each | In proportion to stratum size, or equal numbers weighted afterwards | Whole clusters |
| Use when | The population is already in groups of different sizes | The groups look like small copies of the whole, and cost matters |

A quick test: *is there little variation within groups and a lot between them?* Use stratified. *Is it the other way round?* Use cluster.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Stratifying a bank's customers into retail, small business and corporate makes sense because they behave very differently. Treating each branch as a cluster of a mixed customer base, and surveying all customers in a few branches, is cheaper and works if branches resemble one another.

self_check.prompt_text: Customers fall into three very different segments of different sizes. Which method, and how would you set sample sizes?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Stratified sampling, with the number drawn from each segment proportional to its share of customers (or equal numbers, weighted later by share).

payload.title: Sampling distributions and standard error
payload.core_explanation_md:
Take one sample and you get one mean. Take another sample of the same size and you get a different mean. If you could take **every** possible sample of that size, the collection of all their means is the **sampling distribution of the mean**. The same idea gives a sampling distribution for a median or a proportion.

Two facts to carry away:

- the sample means cluster around the population mean (their average equals it), and they are less spread out than the individual values;
- the standard deviation of that distribution is the **standard error**. It measures how far a sample mean is likely to stray from the truth by chance alone.

Smaller standard error means a better, more reliable estimator.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Do not confuse the two spreads. The standard deviation describes how individual items vary. The standard error describes how the sample *means* vary. The second is always smaller for n greater than 1.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the standard error of the mean measure, in one sentence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: How much sample means vary from sample to sample, because of chance, around the population mean.

payload.title: Standard error of the mean and the z value of a sample mean
payload.core_explanation_md:
For samples of size n from a population with mean mu and standard deviation sigma (infinite population, or sampling with replacement), the sampling distribution of the mean has the same centre as the population and a smaller spread:

- centre: mu of x-bar equals mu;
- spread: the standard error is sigma divided by the square root of n.

To find how likely a sample mean is to fall beyond a given value, measure the distance in standard errors and use the standard normal table: z is the sample mean minus mu, divided by the standard error. Areas on opposite sides of zero are added, on the same side subtracted.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The z value is unit-free, so the same table serves rupees, days or percentages. If the population is normal, this works for any n. If it is not, use it when n is at least 30 (central limit theorem).

variables.name: Standard normal value of the sample mean

assumptions: Population infinite, or sampling with replacement (otherwise apply the finite population multiplier).
Population normal, or n large enough (at least 30) for the central limit theorem.
common_errors: Dividing by n instead of its square root.
Using sigma instead of the standard error as the denominator of z.
Adding table areas for two z values on the same side of zero instead of subtracting.

self_check.prompt_text: sigma = 40 and n = 25. What is the standard error, and how many standard errors above mu is a sample mean 12 above mu?

payload.title: The central limit theorem in practice
payload.core_explanation_md:
Real populations are rarely bell-shaped: loan sizes, deposit balances and claim amounts are usually skewed. The **central limit theorem** rescues us:

- whatever the shape of the population, the mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean;
- as the sample size grows, the **shape** of the sampling distribution of the mean approaches the normal curve.

In practice you do not need an enormous sample. Use the normal approximation when **n is at least 30**; for fairly well-behaved populations even about 15 may be enough. The payoff: you can make probability statements about a sample mean without knowing the shape of the population.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The theorem is about sample means (and sums), not about individual values. A skewed population stays skewed; it is the distribution of the averages that becomes bell-shaped.

self_check.prompt_text: A population of account balances is heavily skewed. Can you use the normal table for the mean of a random sample of 50 accounts? Why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes. With n of at least 30 the central limit theorem makes the sampling distribution of the mean approximately normal, whatever the population shape.

payload.title: Finite population multiplier and the 5 per cent rule
payload.core_explanation_md:
Sampling **without replacement** from a **finite** population gives more information per item than the plain formula credits, because each item drawn leaves fewer unknowns. The standard error is multiplied by a correction, the **finite population multiplier**, which is below 1.

The **sampling fraction** n/N tells you whether it matters. If the sample is a tiny share of the population, the multiplier is almost 1 and can be dropped. The accepted rule: when n/N is **less than 0.05**, skip the multiplier.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Notice what precision depends on. With the multiplier dropped, the standard error depends only on n, the absolute size of the sample, not on how big a slice of the population it is. A sample of 400 from a very large population is as precise as 400 from a larger one.

assumptions: Population finite and sampling without replacement.
The multiplier may be omitted when n/N is less than 0.05.
common_errors: Applying the multiplier when sampling with replacement.
Using N - n over N instead of N - n over N - 1.
Forgetting that the multiplier is inside a square root.

self_check.prompt_text: N = 65 and n = 16. Is the sampling fraction large enough that the multiplier matters, and what is the multiplier?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sampling fraction 16/65, about 0.25, is above 0.05, so it matters. Multiplier = square root of 49/64 = 7/8 = 0.875.

payload.title: More sample, less error: diminishing returns
payload.core_explanation_md:
Because the standard error is sigma over the square root of n, it falls as the sample grows, but ever more slowly:

| Sample size | Standard error when sigma = 100 |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | 31.63 |
| 100 | 10 |

A tenfold bigger sample cuts the error to roughly one-third, not one-tenth. To halve the error you must **quadruple** the sample.

So the right sample size is a decision, not a maximum: compare the value of the extra precision with the cost of collecting the extra observations.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This is the law of diminishing returns borrowed from economics. A common reasoning error is to think that sampling "half as many" accounts gives half the accuracy. It costs you far less than that, which is why modest samples are used so often.

self_check.prompt_text: If you want the standard error to drop to one-third of its present value, by what factor must the sample size rise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Nine times, because the standard error varies as 1 divided by the square root of n.

payload.title: Every possible sample of two from four loan officers
payload.core_explanation_md: Four loan officers processed 10, 20, 30 and 40 applications on a day. List every sample of two (without replacement), find each sample mean, and check the centre and the spread of the sampling distribution against the population.

worked_steps.description: Population variance (divide by N), from deviations of -15, -5, 5 and 15.
List the samples and their means.
Variance of the sample means, from deviations -10, -5, 0, 0, 5, 10.
Check with the finite-population formula: sigma squared / n times (N - n) / (N - 1).

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Six samples; mean of the sample means 25 applications (equal to the population mean); variance of the sample means 125/3 = 41.67, matching the finite-population formula; standard error about 6.45

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the spread of the six sample means smaller than the spread of the four population values?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Each sample mean averages two values, so highs and lows partly cancel; the sample means lie between 15 and 35 while the population runs from 10 to 40.

payload.title: Is an average deposit of this size surprising?
payload.core_explanation_md: Monthly average deposits per customer at a bank have mean Rs 40,000 and standard deviation Rs 12,000, with a skewed distribution. A random sample of 36 customers is drawn. Find the probability that the sample mean is between Rs 38,000 and Rs 42,000, and that it exceeds Rs 43,000. Use the standard normal areas P(0 < z < 1) = 0.3413 and P(0 < z < 1.5) = 0.4332.

worked_steps.description: The population is skewed but n = 36 is at least 30, so the central limit theorem lets us treat the sample mean as normal.
Opposite sides of zero, so add the two areas.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: 0.6826 (table values; the exact normal area is 0.6827)

worked_steps.description: Half of the area (0.5) lies above the mean, so subtract the area from 0 to 1.5.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: About 68.3 per cent chance the sample mean is within Rs 2,000 of Rs 40,000; about 6.68 per cent chance it exceeds Rs 43,000

self_check.prompt_text: If the sample were 144 customers instead of 36, would the 68 per cent band around Rs 40,000 be wider or narrower?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Narrower: the standard error would be 12,000/12 = Rs 1,000, so the band would be Rs 39,000 to Rs 41,000.

payload.title: Does the finite population multiplier matter? Two checks
payload.core_explanation_md: Case A: a bank audits 16 of 65 branches without replacement, and the branch-level standard deviation of reported cash differences is Rs 120 thousand. Find the standard error of the mean. Case B: a sample of 40 is drawn from 1,000 accounts. Does the multiplier matter?

worked_steps.intermediate_result: 0.246, above 0.05, so the multiplier is needed
0.980, so almost no change; omit it

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Case A: standard error Rs 26.25 thousand (instead of Rs 30 thousand); Case B: the multiplier (0.98) can be ignored because the sampling fraction is below 0.05

self_check.prompt_text: In Case A, what happens to the standard error if all 65 branches are audited?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The multiplier becomes sqrt(0/64) = 0, so there is no sampling error: a census has no standard error.

payload.stem_md: A cheque-printing firm wants to know how many scans a particular type of ink cartridge survives before failing. Which approach is most sensible, and why?

options.text_md: A census, because only complete data is reliable
options.explanation_md: Running every cartridge to failure would destroy the whole stock, so a complete count defeats the purpose.

options.text_md: A sample, because testing every cartridge to failure would destroy the stock and cost too much
options.explanation_md: When examining each item is costly or destructive, a representative sample is tested and the result generalised.

options.text_md: No data collection, because failure is random
options.explanation_md: Random failure is exactly what samples are used to measure.

options.text_md: A census, because the population mean cannot be estimated otherwise
options.explanation_md: The mean can be estimated from a sample, which is the purpose of sampling.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Time, cost and destructive testing are the usual reasons for sampling. A representative sample is examined and the result is generalised to the whole population.

payload.stem_md: Which pair contains only sample quantities?

options.text_md: N and mu
options.explanation_md: Both describe the population.

options.text_md: n and x-bar
options.explanation_md: The sample size and the sample mean are sample quantities (statistics).

options.text_md: mu and sigma
options.explanation_md: Both are population parameters.

options.text_md: N and x-bar
options.explanation_md: N is the population size, so the pair mixes the two.

payload.correct_explanation_md: By convention, Roman letters (n, x-bar) describe the sample and Greek or capital letters (N, mu, sigma) describe the population.

payload.stem_md: A regional head hand-picks five "typical" branches to estimate the satisfaction of all customers in the region. What is the main weakness of this approach?

options.text_md: It is too expensive compared with a census
options.explanation_md: A hand-picked set of five branches is cheap.

options.text_md: It cannot be generalised to any extent at all
options.explanation_md: It may be useful as a pilot; the issue is that its validity cannot be tested rigorously.

options.text_md: It is a probability sample and so cannot be biased
options.explanation_md: Hand-picking is judgement sampling, not probability sampling.

options.text_md: Its representativeness depends on opinion and cannot be tested statistically
options.explanation_md: In judgement sampling the chooser's opinion decides what is included, and rigorous statistical analysis is not possible.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Judgement samples are convenient but rest on the chooser's opinion; rigorous statistical analysis is possible only with random probability samples.

payload.stem_md: A bank assesses customer satisfaction by interviewing only customers who came to the complaints desk during one week. The result is most likely

options.text_md: Unbiased, because the number of customers interviewed was large
options.explanation_md: A large number of respondents does not repair a flawed selection.

options.text_md: Unbiased, because every customer is a bank customer
options.explanation_md: Being in the population is not the same as having a chance of selection.

options.text_md: Biased, because it chooses people likely to have strong negative feelings
options.explanation_md: Selecting those with strong feelings gives a biased sample that does not reflect the overall customer base.

options.text_md: Systematic, because it covers one fixed week
options.explanation_md: Systematic sampling means a fixed interval from a random start; this is a convenience selection.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Choosing people who are likely to hold strong views produces a biased sample, so the result will not reflect all customers.

payload.stem_md: To audit vouchers, an inspector picks a random number between 1 and 25, then examines that voucher and every 25th voucher after it. The method is

options.text_md: Simple random sampling
options.explanation_md: Here the choice of every 25th after a start fixes which vouchers are together; not every sample is equally likely.

options.text_md: Cluster sampling
options.explanation_md: No clusters are drawn.

options.text_md: Systematic sampling
options.explanation_md: A random start followed by a fixed interval is systematic sampling.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Taking every k-th item after a random start is systematic sampling.

payload.stem_md: Daily ATM withdrawal data are sampled by taking every seventh day. Why could this give a misleading average?

options.text_md: Because systematic sampling gives items unequal chances of selection
options.explanation_md: Each day has an equal chance; the problem is the pattern.

options.text_md: Because a seven-day interval can match a weekly cycle in withdrawals and pick the same weekday each time
options.explanation_md: When the interval coincides with a pattern in the population, the sample is biased.

options.text_md: Because the sample size is always too small
options.explanation_md: The size is not the issue.

options.text_md: Because replacement is not allowed
options.explanation_md: Replacement has nothing to do with the interval problem.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The risk in systematic sampling is that the interval matches a periodic pattern in the data. A weekly interval on a weekly cycle always lands on the same weekday.

payload.stem_md: A bank groups its branches by region. Within each region, branches are very similar, but regions differ a lot. The bank wants a sample of branches. Which method suits this population best?

options.explanation_md: Cluster sampling suits groups that are alike each other with wide variation inside.

options.explanation_md: The sample size is a count, not a mean.

options.text_md: The standard error
options.explanation_md: The standard error measures spread, not centre.

options.text_md: The population mean
options.explanation_md: The sampling distribution of the mean is centred on the population mean.

options.text_md: The largest value in the population
options.explanation_md: Sample means lie within the population range, centred on the mean.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The mean of the sampling distribution of the mean is the population mean.

payload.stem_md: The standard error of the mean is best described as

options.text_md: The standard deviation of individual values in the population
options.explanation_md: That is the population standard deviation, sigma.

options.text_md: The standard deviation of the distribution of sample means
options.explanation_md: It measures how far sample means vary around the population mean through chance.

options.text_md: The mistake made by a careless interviewer
options.explanation_md: It refers to chance variation in sampling, not blunders.

options.text_md: The sample mean minus the population mean in one particular sample
options.explanation_md: That is the sampling error in a single sample, not the standard deviation of all of them.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean.

payload.stem_md: Loan sizes are strongly skewed. A random sample of 64 loans is drawn repeatedly, and the sample mean is computed each time. The distribution of these sample means will be

options.text_md: Skewed in the same way as the loan sizes
options.explanation_md: The shape of the means changes with n; it does not copy the population.

options.text_md: Approximately normal, with mean equal to the population mean
options.explanation_md: By the central limit theorem, with n of at least 30 the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal.

options.text_md: Approximately normal, but centred below the population mean
options.explanation_md: The mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean.

options.text_md: Impossible to describe without knowing the population shape
options.explanation_md: The theorem exists to avoid exactly that requirement.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The central limit theorem says the sampling distribution of the mean approaches the normal distribution as n grows, whatever the population shape, and its mean is the population mean.

payload.stem_md: Which sample can safely be treated without the finite population multiplier?

options.text_md: 30 accounts from a population of 100
options.explanation_md: The sampling fraction is 0.30, well above 0.05.

options.text_md: 20 accounts from a population of 200
options.explanation_md: The sampling fraction is 0.10, above 0.05.

options.text_md: 9 accounts from a population of 60
options.explanation_md: The sampling fraction is 0.15, above 0.05.

options.text_md: 50 accounts from a population of 2,000
options.explanation_md: The sampling fraction is 0.025, below 0.05, so the multiplier may be omitted.

payload.correct_explanation_md: When the sampling fraction n/N is less than 0.05 the finite population multiplier is close to 1 and need not be used.

payload.stem_md: A researcher quadruples the sample size, keeping everything else the same. The standard error of the mean will

options.text_md: Fall to one-quarter of its value
options.explanation_md: It varies with the square root of n, not with n.

options.text_md: Fall to one-half of its value
options.explanation_md: The square root of 4 is 2, so the standard error is divided by 2.

options.text_md: Remain unchanged
options.explanation_md: The standard error depends on n.

options.text_md: Double
options.explanation_md: A larger sample reduces the standard error.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The standard error is sigma divided by the square root of n. Multiplying n by 4 divides the standard error by 2.

payload.stem_md: Loan balances have a population standard deviation of Rs 48 thousand. For random samples of 64 loans, what is the standard error of the mean, in Rs thousand?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Standard error = sigma / sqrt(n) = 48 / 8 = 6.

worked_solution_steps.description: Square root of the sample size.

payload.stem_md: Balances have mean Rs 5,000 and standard deviation Rs 500. A random sample of 25 accounts has a mean of Rs 5,250. How many standard errors is the sample mean above the population mean (the z value)?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.stem_md: The population standard deviation of a variable is 30. How large a sample is needed (with replacement) for the standard error of the mean to be 2?
payload.correct_explanation_md: From 2 = 30 / sqrt(n): sqrt(n) = 15, so n = 225.

worked_solution_steps.description: Solve for the square root of n.

payload.stem_md: Sampling is without replacement from a population of N = 26 items with a sample of n = 10. What is the finite population multiplier?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 4 decimal places.

payload.stem_md: A sample of 40 accounts is drawn from a population of 1,000. What is the sampling fraction, as a decimal?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 3 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Sampling fraction = n / N = 40 / 1,000 = 0.040, which is below 0.05.

payload.stem_md: A population has four values: 8, 14, 20 and 26. All possible samples of size 2 are drawn without replacement and the mean of each sample is found. What is the mean of these sample means?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean: (8 + 14 + 20 + 26) / 4 = 68 / 4 = 17.
